📌 Rehypothecation: When One Collateral Base Works Twice

Main Points
⏺ In DeFi, the same collateral can indirectly back multiple obligations
⏺ It boosts capital efficiency but increases systemic fragility
⏺ This post explains how “leverage on top of leverage” forms

1️⃣ How It Happens — you post collateral, borrow against it, then reuse the borrowed asset as collateral elsewhere.
2️⃣ Why People Do It — yield strategies and capital efficiency: more output from the same base.
3️⃣ Where Risk Lives — a price drop can trigger cascading liquidations across layers.
4️⃣ Why It Matters — calm markets hide the links; stress markets push correlations toward 1.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — count how many collateral layers your strategy has and model a sharp drawdown.

Final Thoughts

Rehypothecation is an accelerator. It adds efficiency, but it makes systems brittle when markets break.

🛢 France’s Red Alert: Oil, Rates, and a Museum Budget

France is now borrowing at levels it hasn’t seen since the eurozone debt crisis, and the bond market has started speaking louder than any minister.

Valeurs actuelles points out the blunt fact: yields on 30‑year French bonds pushed past 4.7% last week, hitting around 4.74% — a record in the current cycle and a clear “red signal” for public finances already under heavy strain. 

Total public debt has climbed above €3.5 trillion, more than 110% of GDP, and the cost of servicing it is rising as old cheap bonds roll over into a world of higher rates. 

Every tenth of a point added to long‑term yields is money that won’t go to hospitals, schools, or social programs; it goes to paying for yesterday’s deficits.

This is how the ultimatum sounds: France faces rising interest bills, a deficit still near 5% of GDP, and projections that debt could reach 130% of GDP by the end of the decade unless spending is cut or taxes go up. 

The debt is not abstract. INSEE and the Treasury are already warning that interest payments alone could jump from roughly €52 billion to nearly €60 billion between 2025 and 2026, and further toward €120 billion by 2030 if rates stay high. 

That is pure outflow — money that buys no teacher, no nurse, no new infrastructure.

France is paying for a long mix: structurally high social spending, decades of political fear around reform, the COVID shock, the energy crisis, and now a global rate environment that punishes weak growth and messy politics. 

If yields stay near 4.7% on the long end, the budget math will not care how many speeches are made about sovereignty or social justice. It will force cuts, freezes, or new taxes.

Oil spikes from the Iran war and Red Sea blockades push the story further. Higher energy costs hit households and industry, cut into growth, and make debt ratios worse just as markets demand more yield for holding French paper. 

A country that once sold itself as a social model now risks sliding into a “museum state” budget: keeping the façade of services while quietly cannibalizing investment to feed interest payments.
